title: Is @FunctionalInterface mandatory, can a functional interface extend another non-functional interface, and can it have default and static methods while lambdas still work?
keyPoints: @FunctionalInterface is NOT mandatory: any interface with exactly one abstract method works as a lambda target.
The annotation documents intent and provides a compile-time guard against accidentally adding a second abstract method.
Without the annotation, adding a second abstract method silently breaks all lambda usage sites across the codebase.
A functional interface can extend another interface if the combined result still has exactly one abstract method.
Default methods provide composition (and, andThen) and static methods provide factories (Predicate.not, Comparator.comparing).
Lambdas implement only the single abstract method; default and static methods are inherited automatically.
This is the same principle as @Override: technically optional but prevents subtle bugs and should always be used.

s1_definition.oneliner: @FunctionalInterface is optional but strongly recommended as a compile-time guard; any SAM interface works as a lambda target, can extend other interfaces, and can have unlimited default and static methods.
s1_definition.profdef:
- **Not mandatory**: any interface with exactly one abstract method IS a functional interface regardless of the annotation.
- **Compile-time guard**: with @FunctionalInterface, accidentally adding a second abstract method causes an immediate compile error at the interface definition.
- **Without it**: the error appears at every lambda usage site, far from the actual mistake, making debugging harder.
- **Can extend**: a functional interface can extend another interface as long as the combined abstract method count is exactly one.
- **Default methods**: enable composition patterns like `and()`, `or()`, `andThen()` without breaking the SAM rule.
- **Static methods**: enable factory patterns like `Predicate.not()`, `Comparator.comparing()` on the interface itself.
s1_definition.analogy: The @FunctionalInterface stamp on a bank form is like the ISO Certified label. The form works without it, but the stamp guarantees quality control. If someone accidentally adds a second blank field (abstract method), the quality inspector (compiler) catches it immediately at the form design stage. Without the stamp, the mistake passes through design and only surfaces when a customer (caller) tries to fill in the form (lambda compilation fails far from the source).

sections.s3_flow:
```text
  @FunctionalInterface (compile-time guard)
  ─────────────────────────────────────────
  interface AccountValidator {
      boolean validate(String id);      ← 1 abstract (lambda target)
      default AccountValidator and(...) ← does NOT count
      static AccountValidator always()  ← does NOT count
      String toString();                ← Object method, does NOT count
  }

  With annotation:    Without annotation:
  ┌──────────────┐    ┌──────────────┐
  │ Add 2nd      │    │ Add 2nd      │
  │ abstract →   │    │ abstract →   │
  │ COMPILE ERROR│    │ Compiles OK  │
  │ at INTERFACE │    │ Breaks at    │
  │              │    │ every LAMBDA │
  └──────────────┘    └──────────────┘
```
sections.s6_takeaway:
The @FunctionalInterface annotation is not mandatory. Any interface with exactly one abstract method is a functional interface that lambdas can target. However, the annotation is strongly recommended because it provides compile-time safety. If someone accidentally adds a second abstract method, the compiler immediately reports the error at the interface definition. Without the annotation, the error appears at every lambda usage site across the codebase, far from the actual mistake.

In Rajesh's brokerage fee service, the FeeCalculator functional interface has one abstract method (calculate), default composition methods (withMinimum, withMaximum), and static factory methods (percentageFee, flatFee). Each factory returns a lambda. Each default method wraps the current lambda in a new lambda that adds a rule. This creates a composable pipeline: `FeeCalculator.percentageFee(0.001).withMinimum(20).withMaximum(2500)` produces a fee calculator from composing one-line lambdas without any class hierarchy.

A functional interface can extend another interface as long as the combined result has exactly one abstract method. If the parent has an abstract method, the child must override it as default. Default and static methods do not count toward the SAM limit because they have implementations.

Remember one sentence: @FunctionalInterface is optional but always use it, just like @Override, because it catches design mistakes at the source.
